resources.string: Recommended starting value: %1$s.

Controls how the completed image is enlarged: nearest keeps sharp pixel edges, while linear blends neighbouring pixels. Linear can soften text and pixel art without adding game detail. Use nearest for crisp pixels or linear if you prefer a smoother image.
Turns the game sound output on or off. Muting does not raise the emulated clock or guarantee faster gameplay. Keep sound enabled normally and disable it when you need silent play.

Sets the shape of the displayed image: auto uses the core ratio, pixel uses square source pixels, and the other choices force a screen ratio. Forcing 4:3 or 16:9 can stretch characters and does not reveal extra scenery. Start with auto and use pixel for uncorrected pixel proportions.

Chooses automatic game aspect detection, forced 4:3 or 16:9, full-area stretch, or raw image proportions. Forcing a ratio can distort the picture and does not by itself expand the 3D camera. Use auto first and change it only when the game or your display needs a different shape.

Selects Vulkan or OpenGL for Dolphin graphics rendering. Driver compatibility, shader stutter and GPU load vary by game and device, so neither backend is fastest everywhere. Start with Vulkan and compare OpenGL if a game has rendering errors or poor frame pacing.

Multiplies the internal 3D rendering resolution before the image reaches the screen. Higher values sharpen geometry but increase GPU work and memory use; original textures do not gain new detail. Start at 1x and raise it only while gameplay remains at full speed.

Expands the 3D projection of games designed for a narrower screen. Objects may disappear at the edges, and HUD or effects can become misaligned because the game still expects its original view. Leave it off unless this particular game looks correct with the hack.

Smooths polygon edges by sampling each rendered pixel multiple times. Larger sample counts cost GPU bandwidth and memory and may be unavailable on a backend. Start with 1x, which disables MSAA, and increase it only if jagged edges bother you and speed stays stable.

Improves texture clarity on surfaces viewed at steep angles, such as roads and floors. Higher filtering levels add GPU work, and forcing a level may change the intended texture appearance. Keep the default first and try a higher level when angled textures look blurry.

Keeps game-selected texture filtering or forces nearest or linear filtering. Nearest sharpens texels, while linear blends them and may blur UI or alter effects. Use the default for compatibility and force a filter only for a visual preference you have checked in the game.

Selects specialized shaders, hybrid or exclusive ubershaders, or skipping draws while shaders compile. Specialized can stutter on new effects; ubershaders need more GPU power, and skip can show missing objects. Start with specialized, try hybrid for compilation stutter, and avoid skip when image completeness matters.

Keeps compiled shader data for reuse between launches. It uses storage and can shorten repeated compilation, but new effects or driver changes may still require shaders to compile. Leave it enabled unless you are diagnosing a cache-related rendering problem.

Waits for cached shader compilation before gameplay begins. This can reduce early shader stutter but lengthens the initial loading screen and cannot eliminate every new shader pause. Enable it when smoother starts matter more than the shortest boot time.

Synchronizes presented frames with the display refresh. It can reduce tearing but may add latency or uneven pacing when the game cannot keep up. Try it for visible tearing and leave it off if responsiveness or pacing becomes worse.

Moves supported graphics backend work onto an additional thread. This can reduce CPU bottlenecks but adds synchronization and depends on the device driver. Keep it enabled normally and disable it when investigating driver crashes or graphics instability.

Skips CPU reads or writes to the embedded frame buffer used by some game effects. It can avoid expensive GPU synchronization but may break picking, collisions, visibility tests or other game logic. Keep the default for speed and turn it off if a game needs those frame-buffer accesses.

Keeps embedded frame-buffer copies as GPU textures instead of also writing them to emulated RAM. This usually avoids readback costs, but some games need RAM copies for effects or logic. Leave it enabled first and disable it for missing effects or a known game-specific requirement.

Keeps external frame-buffer copies on the GPU instead of copying their pixels into emulated RAM. It reduces transfer work but can break games that read or modify those RAM images. Start enabled and disable it if a game has missing video or incorrect frame-buffer effects.

Delays writing frame-buffer copies to RAM until they are needed. This can reduce stalls but relies on timing assumptions that some games do not tolerate. Leave it enabled first and disable it when frame-buffer effects or game logic are incorrect.

Presents external frame-buffer copies immediately instead of waiting for normal scanout. This can reduce latency but may expose intermediate images or flicker and also skips duplicate presentations. Leave it off unless you have verified that the game displays correctly with immediate presentation.

Avoids presenting identical external frame-buffer copies repeatedly. It can reduce work in games running below the display refresh rate, but frame pacing can become less consistent. Keep it enabled for efficiency and disable it if repeated-frame pacing looks smoother.

Creates embedded frame-buffer copies at the selected internal resolution. Effects that use those copies can look sharper, but memory use grows and some games expect native-sized copies. Keep it enabled and disable it if an effect breaks when resolution is raised.

Ignores changes to the embedded frame-buffer pixel format. This avoids conversion work but can give effects incorrect colours or precision. Keep the default initially and turn it off when a game requires accurate format changes.

Chooses how thoroughly texture data is checked for changes before a cached texture is reused. Safe checks more data at greater CPU cost, while fast can miss updates and show stale or flickering textures. Start with balanced and switch to safe when textures fail to update correctly.

Moves supported console texture decoding from the CPU to the GPU. It may help a CPU bottleneck but can increase GPU pressure and requires backend support. Leave it off initially and compare it in the same scene before keeping it enabled.

Uses a faster approximation for depth calculations. It can reduce graphics work but may misplace effects or surfaces that depend on precise depth. Keep it enabled normally and disable it when depth-related visual errors appear.

Disables emulation of the GPU bounding-box feature. It can reduce GPU work, but games that use bounding-box results may lose effects or break gameplay. Keep the default for ordinary games and turn this option off for games that require the feature.

Rounds 2D vertices and viewport sizes to whole pixels at increased internal resolutions. This can fix seams or misaligned sprites but changes positioning and has no effect at native resolution. Enable it only for visible 2D alignment problems after increasing resolution.

Removes game fog from rendered scenes. Distant objects become easier to see, but the intended atmosphere and hidden scene boundaries can change. Leave it off for the original appearance and enable it only as a visual preference.

Removes the console copy filter that normally softens the final image. The picture can become sharper, but games may show more aliasing or lose an intended blur effect. Keep it enabled for a crisp picture or disable it to retain the original filter.

Uses higher colour precision instead of the original lower-precision rendering. This can reduce colour banding but changes dithering and effects that depend on console precision. Keep it enabled for cleaner gradients and disable it when an effect needs original colour behaviour.

Calculates supported lighting per pixel instead of using the original vertex-based result. Lighting can appear smoother, but GPU work increases and the game may look different from the console. Leave it off unless you prefer the effect and have spare GPU performance.

Loads installed high-resolution texture replacements for this game. Packs can improve texture detail but use storage, memory and loading time, and incorrect packs can show wrong artwork. Enable it only after installing a compatible texture pack.

Preloads replacement textures into memory rather than loading each texture when first needed. It can reduce in-game loading hitches but raises memory use and may lengthen startup. Leave it off on memory-limited devices and enable it only with a pack that fits comfortably.

Includes frame-buffer texture data in save states. This helps restore missing or upscaled effects after loading but increases state size and save or load time. Keep it enabled unless smaller states matter more than exact visual restoration.

Chooses the ARM64 JIT, cached interpreter or plain interpreter for the emulated CPU. Interpreters are useful for diagnosis but are usually much slower and can prevent full-speed gameplay. Use JIT normally and try an interpreter only for a specific compatibility investigation.

Runs emulated CPU and GPU work on separate host threads. It can improve throughput but introduces synchronization differences that some games cannot tolerate. Keep it enabled for normal play and disable it for game-specific instability or timing problems.

Enables more complete emulation of CPU virtual-memory translation. Some games need it to work correctly, while others gain no visual benefit and may run more slowly. Leave it off unless a game requires MMU support.

Emulates CPU cache behaviour more accurately. This can fix games that depend on cache details but adds CPU overhead without improving ordinary image quality. Leave it off unless it resolves a known compatibility problem.

Emulates floating-point result flags used by certain CPU instructions. It may fix game calculations but adds work when those flags are needed. Leave it off unless a game has a known requirement for accurate result flags.

Preserves more accurate floating-point NaN behaviour in the emulated CPU. This targets unusual game calculations rather than image sharpness and can add execution cost. Leave it off unless a game requires this floating-point compatibility fix.

Emulates fused floating-point multiply-add results more accurately. It can resolve calculation differences but may cost CPU time and does not directly raise resolution. Leave it off unless incorrect game behaviour is fixed by accurate fused operations.

Uses faster host-memory access paths for the emulated CPU. It can reduce CPU overhead, but disabling it may help diagnose a memory-access compatibility issue. Keep it enabled unless troubleshooting identifies it as the cause of a problem.

Removes normal disc read timing limits. Loading may finish sooner, but games that depend on original disc timing can behave incorrectly. Leave it off for compatibility and enable it only after checking the game through loading transitions.

Changes the emulated CPU clock relative to the original console. Raising it may reduce original game slowdown but increases host CPU load, while lowering it can alter timing or slow game logic. Use 100 percent first and adjust only for a tested game-specific need.

Uses high-level emulation for the console audio processor instead of low-level DSP emulation. HLE is generally lighter, while LLE may help unusual audio behaviour and needs more processing time. Keep HLE enabled unless a game requires the low-level audio path.

Uses a recompiler for low-level DSP emulation instead of its interpreter. This mainly matters when DSP HLE is off; the interpreter can be much slower. Keep DSP JIT enabled unless diagnosing an LLE audio problem.

Runs low-level DSP work on a separate thread. It may distribute CPU load better, but synchronization changes can cause audio or timing problems and it does not benefit DSP HLE in the same way. Leave it off initially and test it only when using LLE.

Selects Cubeb or OpenSL ES for sound output to Android. Device support, latency and underrun behaviour can differ, without changing the game music itself. Start with Cubeb and try OpenSL ES if sound fails or repeatedly crackles.

Adjusts the game audio level before output. Lower values make sound quieter without slowing the game, while high levels can make an already loud mix uncomfortable. Start at the default and reduce the level to suit your headphones or speakers.

Sets the target audio buffer duration in milliseconds. A larger buffer can absorb brief scheduling delays but increases audio latency; a smaller one responds sooner but may crackle. Start at 80 ms and increase it only when underruns remain audible.

Keeps audio pitch steadier when emulation runs at a speed other than normal. Time stretching can add processing cost, latency or audible artifacts, especially during large speed changes. Enable it if changed music pitch bothers you and compare the result at your chosen speed.

Fills short gaps in audio output instead of leaving them silent. It can make brief slowdowns less disruptive but cannot restore missing game speed and may alter the sound during a stall. Keep it enabled normally and disable it when comparing audio timing or artifacts.

Sets the target emulation speed relative to normal gameplay. Faster targets require more device performance and change game pacing and audio; slower targets intentionally slow the game. Use 1.0 for normal play and change it only for deliberate fast or slow motion.

Selects the language reported by the emulated GameCube console. Only languages included in the game are available, and some releases ignore this preference. Choose your preferred supported language and use the game menu if it offers its own selection.

Selects the emulated Wii Remote, Remote with Nunchuk, or Classic Controller attachment. The choice changes which buttons and sticks the game receives, and unsupported controllers may not work in that game. Choose the controller type listed by the game rather than enabling every attachment.

Enables the emulated Wii Remote speaker feature. Games can use it for extra sound cues, while disabling it may silence those cues or make the mix less complete. Keep it enabled unless remote-speaker audio causes a problem in the game.

Skips a selected number of rendered frames between displayed frames. This can reduce rendering work on a slow device but makes motion less smooth and does not make game logic more accurate. Keep it at zero and increase it only if the game otherwise cannot maintain speed.

Controls whether mGBA detects or removes emulated CPU idle loops, or leaves them untouched. Avoiding idle work can help speed, but forced removal may affect games with unusual timing. Use detect first and choose ignore when investigating timing or compatibility problems.

Allows opposite directional buttons, such as left and right, to reach the game together. Original controls normally prevent these combinations, and some games react unpredictably to them. Leave it off unless a specific homebrew program or input test needs opposing directions.

Selects the Game Boy audio high-pass filter: accurate hardware behaviour, DC-offset removal only, or no filter. The choices change low-frequency sound and transients, and turning filtering off can introduce a DC offset. Use accurate for normal play and compare other modes only for a specific audio preference.

Adds emulated Game Boy hardware interference noise at the selected level. Higher values make background hardware noise more audible rather than improving music fidelity. Keep it at zero for clean sound or raise it slightly if you want the original hardware character.

Chooses the monochrome shades used for Game Boy games, including DMG, grey, Pocket and Light looks. It changes colours only and does not add Game Boy Color graphics or improve speed. Choose the palette you find most readable or closest to your preferred original screen.

Adjusts Game Boy Color colour curves to approximate the original display response. Colours can look less vivid than raw RGB output, but disabling correction may exaggerate colours designed for the handheld screen. Keep it enabled for a console-like appearance or disable it if you prefer the raw palette.

Removes the NES per-scanline sprite limit. It can reduce hardware-style sprite flicker but may reveal sprites that the game intentionally hides or change visual effects. Leave it off for original behaviour and enable it only after checking the game scenes that use many sprites.

Uses the faster SNES picture-processing implementation instead of the more precise path. It reduces emulation work and enables HD Mode 7, but some timing-sensitive effects may render differently. Keep it on initially and turn it off for graphics problems that need the accurate PPU.

Uses the faster SNES audio DSP implementation. It can reduce CPU work but may differ from the accurate path in timing-sensitive audio behaviour. Start enabled and disable it if a game has reproducible audio errors.

Controls randomization of memory and registers at startup. Low resembles normal SNES startup, high stresses uninitialized-memory assumptions, and none uses constant values that some old homebrew expects. Use low for games and change it only for development or a known startup incompatibility.

Emulates the horizontal blending used by the SNES image path, including supported pseudo-transparency effects. Blending can make these effects look correct but softens pixel edges. Leave it off for sharp pixels or enable it when a game relies on blended transparency.

Removes SNES sprite limits in the fast PPU. It can reduce flicker or disappearing sprites but may expose objects or change effects that rely on hardware limits. Leave it off for original graphics and enable it only after checking busy scenes.

Includes image lines normally hidden by the SNES overscan area. More border content becomes visible, but some games put blank lines or garbage there. Leave it off for the usual cropped view and enable it when you need those extra lines.

Applies the core fixes for selected bugs that also existed in original games. These can improve playability but intentionally change behaviour from unmodified hardware execution. Leave it off for faithful behaviour or enable it if you want the supported game bug fixes.

Raises the rendering resolution of Mode 7 backgrounds in the fast PPU. Roads and rotating planes can look sharper, but higher scales increase CPU and memory work and do not upscale every sprite. Start at 1x and raise it only when the game keeps full speed.

Changes the emulated SNES main CPU speed relative to normal hardware. Higher values can reduce original game slowdown but require more host work and can break timing. Start at 100 percent and adjust only for a game you have tested through different scenes.

Changes the emulated SA-1 coprocessor clock in cartridges that contain it. Higher values may reduce slowdown in those games but increase CPU load and can change timing; other cartridges gain nothing. Use 100 percent first and raise it only for a tested SA-1 game.

Changes the emulated Super FX coprocessor clock in cartridges that contain it. Higher values can make supported 3D scenes smoother but add CPU work and may alter timing or game speed. Start at 100 percent and increase cautiously only for Super FX games.

Makes SNES CPU multiplication and division results available without their original delay. This supports some old ROM hacks but changes hardware timing rather than providing a general performance upgrade. Leave it off unless a particular ROM hack needs immediate math results.

Changes how the fast PPU presents interlaced SNES images. It can reduce interlace flicker but changes the appearance of alternating fields and may soften or alter fine details. Keep it enabled first and disable it if you prefer the original interlaced presentation.

Allows video RAM access at times when real SNES hardware would block it. Some old ROM hacks require this inaccurate behaviour, and it can also reduce fast-PPU performance. Leave it off unless a known incompatible ROM hack needs unrestricted VRAM access.

Applies perspective correction to high-resolution Mode 7 backgrounds in the fast PPU. It can make sloped planes more coherent but changes the original sampling and only affects supported Mode 7 scenes. Keep it enabled with HD Mode 7 and disable it if a scene looks wrong.

Adds sampling work when rendering high-resolution Mode 7 backgrounds. It can reduce shimmering but increases CPU cost and is not a general anti-aliasing option for all SNES graphics. Leave it off initially and enable it only if Mode 7 shimmer is visible and speed remains stable.

Reduces HD Mode 7 output to the original scale when the game applies mosaic. This preserves intentionally blocky transitions, while disabling it can change those effects at higher scales. Keep it enabled unless you deliberately prefer the altered high-resolution mosaic appearance.

Uses cubic interpolation for supported SNES DSP sample playback. It changes the tone of sampled music compared with the original Gaussian interpolation and is not an accuracy upgrade. Leave it off for original audio or enable it if you prefer the alternative sound.

Uses separate shadow memory for the SNES DSP echo buffer. This can support old ROM hacks that misuse echo RAM but changes how audio writes interact with normal memory. Leave it off unless a specific hack needs this compatibility behaviour.

Delays synchronization with supported SNES cartridge coprocessors until required. It can reduce CPU overhead but relaxes timing coordination and may affect unusual coprocessor behaviour. Keep it enabled first and disable it for a reproducible coprocessor compatibility problem.

Prefers high-level emulation for cartridge coprocessors when available. It can reduce CPU work but is less precise; disabling it uses low-level emulation when the required firmware is available. Leave it enabled normally and try low-level emulation for a known compatibility issue.

Simulates extra frames with state rollback to reduce the input delay shown on screen. More frames demand substantially more CPU work and can cause slowdowns or state-related incompatibilities. Leave it off first and try one frame only when the device has enough spare performance.

Simulates different analogue SNES video connections, from RF and composite to cleaner S-Video and RGB looks. These filters add colour blending, artifacts or processing work instead of increasing the original game detail. Choose none for clean pixels or select a connection style for the visual effect you prefer.
